paragraphs: Advertising and promotions managers do not just come up with creative ideas: the work packs audience evidence, verifiable claims, creative material, media selection, budget, and delivery specifications into one campaign decision chain, with responsibility for launch readiness and performance review. Product licensing, legal opinion, platform review, and the organisation's final commitment remain with the responsible authorized parties.

Start with a small exercise that can be completed within a day: write a one-page creative brief, three evidence-based claims, two material versions, a media budget, and a pre-launch checklist for a fictional product, then simulate one round of performance reading and review. Record how many claims you changed for lack of evidence, whether you can explain the budget trade-offs, and whether you are willing to push approvals repeatedly among brand, legal, and media. This is only an entry-level slice and cannot represent campaign management competence or replace collaboration and outcome responsibility in a real project.

Observable signals that someone may fit better include: being able to explain the target audience, the basis for claims, channel limits, cost, and the measurement approach beyond aesthetic preference; being willing to cut or revise creative you personally like according to brand and compliance rules; habitually writing budgets, material versions, and approval status into records that can be handed over; and checking the measurement basis before drawing conclusions when metrics move. Be cautious if you tend to exaggerate selling points, ignore qualifiers, chase clicks without checking misleading risk, or dislike cross-team negotiation and repeated revision.
This is exploratory advice; it must be checked together with your interests, hands-on task experience, and the job conditions of the target market, and cannot replace your own judgment.

The core exchange of this work is turning product, audience, and budget information into a launchable, reviewable advertising or promotions campaign: set the audience and goals, write claims that can be substantiated, organize creative and media, hold the budget and compliance boundaries, then review with metrics. Judging fit should depend on whether you are willing to revise repeatedly along this chain and leave a basis for each change, not just on whether you like creative work; interest and personality assessments serve only as clues.

O*NET 11-2011.00 defines advertising and promotions managers as planning, directing, or coordinating advertising policies and programs, or producing supporting material such as posters, contests, coupons, and giveaways, to stimulate interest in purchasing a product or service at the department, whole-organisation, or client-account level.

Section heading | Work environment and methods for advertising and promotions managers
Direct answer | Advertising and promotions managers work in advertising and marketing agencies, corporate marketing and brand departments, media organisations, event and public relations firms, and platform and e-commerce teams, serving internal brand leads or external clients; the work centers on briefs, creative and media coordination, budgeting and approval, launch, and review, with time pressure and repeated revision common.
Common organizations and locations | The most common employers in the United States are professional, scientific, and technical services (including advertising and marketing agencies) and the information sector; most roles are office-based and require travel arranged around clients or media.
Work materials and systems | Everyday materials include creative briefs, claim evidence tables, creative material and scripts, media and budget plans, contracts and estimates, delivery specifications and approval records, campaign boards, and performance reviews; common tools include analytics, customer relationship management, design, and office software.
How tasks are organized | Work proceeds in a brief–creative and media–approval–launch–review cycle: first confirm the audience and goals and form the brief, then produce material and the media plan, complete brand, legal, and launch authorization, and after launch evaluate response rates and cost to decide whether to continue, adjust, or stop.
Deadlines and work intensity | Intensity concentrates on campaign launch, final creative, and the delivery window: O*NET work context shows 80% of respondents work more than 40 hours per week and 58% report time pressure once a week or more but not every day.
Collaboration and reporting lines | Work is usually done with copywriters, designers, media, sales, research, and finance, reporting to brand or marketing leads or client-side leads; product licensing, legal opinion, and platform review rest with the responsible authorized parties.
Review and accountability chain | Campaigns must pass brand and legal review, approval by the client or business authorizer, and platform rules checks; budget changes and contract signing follow organizational authority and are documented.
Quality and professional requirements | Quality depends on whether claims are substantiated, material meets specifications, conditions are not hidden, the budget has boundaries, and performance metrics align with the campaign goals.

'Technical tractability' answers only whether a tool is capable of completing a class of tasks; it does not mean an organization has adopted it, nor that jobs have therefore declined. 'Actual organizational adoption' asks whether organizations really put the tool into their processes. items.title: What do employers usually look at when hiring?

values: Task statement and input materials

Fixed case: fictional brand "Qingqi" sugar-free sparkling water (330 ml cans, suggested retail price 5.5 CNY per can, 0 sugar and 0 calories; fictional filed ingredient list: water, erythritol, carbon dioxide, citric acid, food flavouring, sucralose, with no added sucrose or preservatives; the products, channels, and data below are fictional materials for the exercise and do not represent any real company or official statistic). The target market is the fictional city of Linjiang; the target audience is office workers and students aged 18—30 who buy bottled drinks at least once a week; the campaign runs for three months with a total budget of 30 ten-thousand CNY (media 21 ten-thousand, content production 6 ten-thousand, contingency 3 ten-thousand); the primary goal is to raise trial applications to 12,000, and the secondary goal is a cost per acquisition of no more than 25 CNY. Using real client data, personal profiles, unauthorized trademarks, likenesses of real people, or unauthorized music is prohibited.

Simulated performance record supplied with the prompt (fictional): Channel A feed placement ran 8 weeks, with 210 ten-thousand impressions, 5.2 ten-thousand clicks, 4,860 trial applications, and a spend of 12.6 ten-thousand CNY; Channel B short-video creator collaboration ran 6 weeks, with 96 ten-thousand impressions, 3.1 ten-thousand clicks, 2,340 trial applications, and a spend of 6.3 ten-thousand CNY; creative version one (focused on taste and mouthfeel) had a click-through rate of 2.6% on Channel A, and version two (focused on 0 sugar and scenarios) 2.3%; the historical baseline (budget basis not given, and it must not be assumed to be the same budget as this campaign) was 5,600 trial applications and a cost per acquisition of 27.5 CNY.

Materials that must accompany the deliverable: a creative brief (target audience, campaign goals and metrics, reasons for channel choices, budget allocation), three claims with their evidence sources, two creative concepts (a written description or self-made graphics are both acceptable), and a one-page pre-placement checklist (material specifications, permissions, targeting scope, and stop conditions).
Task requirements

Complete the following from the prompt materials: three verifiable claims (each stating its evidence source, conditions of application, and what cannot be promised), two creative concepts, a media and budget plan (channel mix, budget allocation, and stop conditions), and a one-page pre-placement checklist.

Deliver a one-page placement review: use the simulated performance record supplied with the prompt to write the metric readings for each channel and each creative version, compare them item by item against the 12,000-application goal and the 25 CNY cost per acquisition, explain the gaps, possible explanations, limitations, and next actions, and state which conclusions this placement cannot support.
Reference approach

First break the goal into measurable metrics (trial applications, cost per acquisition, channel contribution), then decide the channel and creative combination; annotate each claim with its evidence source and conditions of application - for example, "no added sucrose" should be written so it can be checked against the ingredient list, not as an unprovable promise such as "will not cause weight gain".

A verifiable example deliverable (a fictional exercise reference, not the only answer): a claim could read "the ingredient list in the prompt has no added sucrose, and the sweetening ingredients are erythritol and sucralose; taste preference varies by person, and no health-function claim is made". Channel A click-through about 2.48%, applications/clicks about 9.35%, cost per acquisition 126000 ÷ 4860 ≈ 25.93 CNY; Channel B about 3.23%, 7.55%, 63000 ÷ 2340 ≈ 26.92 CNY, and both are above the 25 CNY target. The two channels' application records add up to 7200, and against the 12000 goal the book gap is 4800; cross-channel de-duplication was not given, so they cannot be called 7200 unique new users. The two channels' media spend is 189000 CNY, giving a cost per acquisition of 26.25 CNY on that basis, excluding production and other costs. The creative one/two click-through rates of 2.6%/2.3% describe only the readings in the prompt; sample size and allocation were not given, so they prove neither causation nor which version brought more applications. The historical 5600 and 27.5 CNY can be listed for comparison, but the budget basis is unknown, and the period and attribution must each be checked. Different channel combinations and creative options must all state their budget, stop conditions, and verifiable basis.
Boundary statement

This exercise verifies brief, claim, creative, and review ability and does not constitute placement advice; the prompt product, channel data, and simulated performance are all fictional materials and must be stored separately from real company data. items.title: Education, training, and qualifications: what are the real thresholds for this occupation?

paragraphs: This page separates general preparation from statutory requirements. The U.S. occupational profiles and the combined BLS entry state that a relevant bachelor's degree and work experience are usually required; this page establishes no uniform mandatory licence requirement, and the specific task, location, industry, and employer conditions must be checked separately.

Positions in mainland China must be checked against actual duties for education, experience, local industry rules, and employer authorization; this page establishes no unified occupational qualification mapping fully corresponding to O*NET11-2011, and cannot be used to assert that no qualification requirement exists.

Training and certification prove only a learning experience and do not equal budget authority, publication authorization, or employer appointment; advertising publication is also bound by local regulations and platform rules.

Practice and work samples should use fictional products and self-made or authorized materials, and must not transfer real client data or personal profiles; claim evidence, material permissions, and placement approval must be completed by someone with the authority within the compliance boundary, with reviewable records kept.

Ability progression is by evidence: from completing briefs and material follow-up under guidance, to independently owning a channel and budget, to mentoring, cross-category campaign management, and team management; it may move toward advertising sales, market research, marketing management, public relations, or art direction, but needs the corresponding client development, research method, category management, or visual training. Entry is split by employer and industry: the United States usually requires a relevant bachelor's degree plus campaign or channel experience, while mainland China mostly follows education and performance conditions set by the employer.
Job titles may differ by company (for example campaign manager, brand manager, account manager); verification should go by actual duties and budget authority rather than the title alone.
